papers.title: AI-augmented discovery of autophagy regulators through mechanistic interpretation of multiomics data.
papers.summary: This paper describes an AI-based approach that mines multiomics datasets (likely combining genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics) to identify new regulators of autophagy. The method emphasizes mechanistic interpretability, meaning the AI model's predictions are linked to biologically meaningful pathways rather than being a black box. This could help researchers pinpoint novel genes or proteins controlling autophagy processes for further experimental validation.
papers.why: Since the PhD project centers on mitophagy and autophagy regulation in neurons, this AI-driven discovery framework could directly inform identification of new molecular targets or pathways relevant to neuronal autophagy, especially when integrated with spatial transcriptomics/metabolomics data.

papers.title: Comparative analysis of neuronal proteolytic pathways reveals neuron-specific and sub-compartmental-specific capacities with aging.
papers.summary: This study compares proteolytic pathways, including autophagy and related protein degradation systems, across different types of neurons and their subcellular compartments. The researchers examine how the capacity of these degradation systems changes with aging, highlighting that neurons are not uniform in how they handle protein turnover. The findings suggest that specific neuron types and specific parts of neurons (like axons versus dendrites or soma) have distinct vulnerabilities or resilience in proteolytic function as animals age.
papers.why: Understanding cell-type-specific and compartment-specific differences in proteolytic and autophagic capacity with aging directly informs the project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, particularly interneurons, across the aging brain.

papers.title: Non-cell autonomous control of presynaptic remodeling by the hypothalamic autophagy-NPY axis.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how autophagy in hypothalamic neurons controls the release of the neuropeptide NPY, which then influences neurons elsewhere in a non-cell autonomous manner. The researchers show that autophagy in one set of neurons can remodel presynaptic structures in connected neural circuits by regulating NPY signaling. This reveals a mechanism where autophagy doesn't just clean up cellular components locally, but actively shapes communication and synaptic architecture between different neurons in the brain.
papers.why: This paper demonstrates a direct mechanistic link between neuronal autophagy and presynaptic remodeling via a specific neuropeptide signaling axis, offering a conceptual framework relevant to how autophagy/mitophagy in one neuronal population could non-cell-autonomously affect synaptic architecture and network properties elsewhere in the brain, including potentially interneuron circuits.

papers.title: The mitophagy-inflammasome axis: a shared pathological hub in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how impaired mitophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria, is linked to activation of the inflammasome, a molecular complex that triggers inflammation, in both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. It argues that faulty mitochondrial clearance leads to buildup of damaged mitochondria, which then trigger chronic neuroinflammation via inflammasome activation. This shared mechanism is proposed as a common pathological hub connecting these two major neurodegenerative diseases, suggesting potential shared therapeutic targets.
papers.why: Since the PhD project centers on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, understanding how disrupted mitophagy drives inflammasome-mediated neurodegeneration provides critical mechanistic context for interpreting spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic changes in neuronal and interneuron populations under disease conditions.

papers.title: A 3-<i>n</i>-butylphthalide-based nanoagent modulates PINK1/Parkin-associated mitophagy signaling in ischemia-reperfusion brain injury.
papers.summary: This paper describes a nanoparticle-based delivery system for 3-n-butylphthalide, a drug being tested for stroke-related brain injury. The nanoagent appears to influence the PINK1/Parkin pathway, which is a key molecular mechanism cells use to identify and remove damaged mitochondria. The study focuses on ischemia-reperfusion injury, a condition where blood flow is restored after being blocked, causing additional tissue damage.
papers.why: This work directly relates to PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy mechanisms in the brain, offering a therapeutic angle that could inform understanding of mitochondrial quality control in neurons relevant to the PhD project.

papers.title: Cell Death in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Targets.
papers.summary: This paper reviews the molecular mechanisms driving cell death in neurodegenerative diseases, covering pathways such as apoptosis, necrosis, and autophagy-related death. It discusses how these mechanisms contribute to disorders like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's disease. The review also highlights potential therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting these cell death pathways to slow or halt neurodegeneration.
papers.why: Since only an abstract without methodological or figure detail is provided, this broad review likely offers useful background on mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neuronal cell death relevant to the PhD project's mechanistic focus.

papers.title: Nutrient Deprivation Enhances Neuronal Survival and Induces Secretion of Protective Extracellular Vesicles.
papers.summary: This paper explores how depriving neurons of nutrients can actually help them survive rather than harm them. The researchers found that this stress condition triggers neurons to release extracellular vesicles (tiny membrane-bound packages) that appear to protect other cells. This suggests a mechanism where cellular stress responses, potentially linked to autophagy, produce beneficial signals that spread to neighboring cells.
papers.why: Since nutrient deprivation and extracellular vesicle secretion are tightly linked to autophagy and mitophagy pathways relevant to neuronal stress adaptation, this work could inform how similar mechanisms operate in interneurons within the brain's spatial context.

papers.title: When Powerhouses Fail and Rust Takes Over: Primary Mitochondrial and Lipid Metabolism Failure with Secondary Iron Accumulation and Lipid Peroxidation in Neurodegeneration with Brain Iron Accumulation.
papers.summary: This paper explores Neurodegeneration with Brain Iron Accumulation (NBIA), a group of disorders where problems in mitochondria and lipid metabolism happen first, before iron builds up and causes damage. The authors argue that iron accumulation and lipid peroxidation (a damaging chain reaction that breaks down fats in cells) are downstream consequences rather than the root cause. This reframes how we think about the disease process, suggesting treatments should target mitochondrial and lipid dysfunction rather than just removing excess iron.
papers.why: Since mitochondrial dysfunction (mitophagy failure) and lipid handling are core to this PhD's focus, understanding how these processes trigger iron accumulation and neurodegeneration could inform how mitophagy defects in neurons relate to broader disease mechanisms measurable via spatial metabolomics.
